bp: A city is not one machine. It is roads, buses, power, water, public services, neighborhoods, buildings, businesses, sensors, residents, and elected decisions all affecting one another. This workshop is about what happens when the Web becomes part of that city machinery: devices report conditions, services publish and consume data, people interact through online systems, and software helps officials decide where to intervene. The abstract frames data as a foundational asset for improving decisions, service operation, and citizen well-being. That is the practical need before any method appears. A city wants to notice congestion, waste, safety risks, energy pressure, service gaps, and public needs early enough to act. The workshop also treats the year-by-year focus as changing, which matters because smart-city work does not have a fixed target. In 2026, the pressure named here is data-driven urban transformation under IoT, AI, agentic AI, integration, and citiverse ideas.
wh: The hard part is that city data is never neutral by itself. A traffic sensor, a service request, a mobility trace, a web search, and a simulated city space each capture only one view of urban life. Decisions made from those views can improve services, but they can also optimize the wrong thing if the data collection or processing method favors what is easy to measure over what residents actually need. The abstract says different processing techniques influence outcomes, which is the central tension. If a city treats data as a simple mirror, it may miss people who are not well represented by connected devices, neighborhoods with sparse reporting, or harms that appear only after a policy is deployed. Integration adds another difficulty: transport, energy, public services, and citizen-facing web systems interact. A choice that reduces delay in one service can shift cost, risk, or inconvenience into another part of the city.
naive: A smart beginner might gather all available city data into one dashboard, add AI predictions, and tell city staff to follow the highest numbers: busiest roads, most reported complaints, largest energy loads, most common citizen requests. That is tempting because it makes the problem look measurable and orderly. It fails because the dashboard does not know what was never measured, why the numbers arose, or who is missing from the data. It also hides the fact that the processing method shapes the conclusion. Counting complaints may reward louder or better-connected groups. Optimizing traffic speed may ignore pedestrians or pollution. A city cannot be improved by treating every data source as equally complete, equally current, and equally aligned with public well-being.
ap: The workshop's core move is not a single algorithm. It creates a research meeting around the city as a connected data system, asking how Web technologies support urban transformation and how different computational choices change urban outcomes. In concrete terms, the subject is the pipeline from urban evidence to urban action: devices and web services produce data; AI systems, agentic systems, and integration tools process it; planners, service operators, or residents use the result to decide what should happen next. The phrase data-driven smart cities should therefore be read carefully. The workshop is not only about collecting more data. It is about examining which data is useful, which method is appropriate, how systems should be joined, and how the resulting choices affect decision-making, service quality, and citizen well-being. Its contribution, as described by the abstract, is to convene work on that whole chain.
mech: The mechanism implied by the abstract begins with many urban sources rather than one tidy table. Internet-connected devices may record conditions; web systems may carry service requests, mobility information, or public interaction; AI tools may classify, forecast, recommend, or summarize; agentic AI means software that can take multi-step actions such as choosing tools, querying services, or coordinating subtasks; the citiverse means a people-centered digital counterpart of the city where urban spaces and interactions can be represented and explored. Those inputs are then integrated, which means they have to be brought into a shared form where separate services can use one another's evidence. After that, processing techniques transform raw observations into signals: a count, a prediction, a ranking, a simulation result, a warning, or a proposed action. Those outputs feed decisions such as which service to adjust, what urban condition to monitor, or where a city might focus resources. The workshop mechanism is the review and comparison of these steps across papers and participants. It asks what the Web contributes as an infrastructure for publishing, connecting, and acting on city data. Because the abstract does not specify experiments, datasets, or a particular system, the honest mechanism is a conceptual and community mechanism: bring together methods, compare their assumptions, and examine their consequences for smart-city decisions.
math: The main mathematical idea is turning messy civic evidence into decisions under constraints. One part is measurement: deciding what a number stands for, such as service delay, congestion, resource use, or citizen well-being. Measurement is already a mathematical choice because it compresses lived conditions into something countable, and whatever is not counted becomes easier to ignore. A second part is probability, meaning a disciplined estimate of what may be true when evidence is partial or noisy. City systems often cannot wait for perfect information, so repeated observations can guide likely demand, risk, or service pressure, while thin evidence should produce caution. A third part is optimization, meaning the search for choices that reduce a defined badness or improve a defined goal, such as shorter delays or better service coverage. The danger is that the chosen score may not equal the public goal. A fourth part is systems integration: matching data formats, timing, and meanings across services so evidence can move without being distorted. If the workshop includes citiverse or agentic-AI settings, the same math also includes simulation and controlled action: represent a city situation, test possible moves, and decide which action is acceptable under cost, safety, and fairness limits.
dots: This workshop sits near several recurring conference ideas in the current data. It connects to time-series and spatiotemporal work because cities are streams over places: traffic, weather, energy, services, and public activity change by hour and neighborhood, so methods must preserve when and where evidence appears. It connects to the optimization concept because urban systems constantly choose under limits: routes, budgets, service priorities, land-use plans, or response policies cannot all be maximized at once. It connects to probability because city decisions often rely on incomplete, delayed, or uneven evidence. It also connects to the LLM agents and tool-use family through the abstract's mention of agentic AI: an urban agent would have to choose tools, retrieve data, coordinate services, and stop before taking unsafe or wasteful action. The unifying pressure is not one method name. It is the need to turn web-connected evidence into accountable action in a real civic environment.
ww: The workshop idea works because cities naturally require crossing boundaries. A traffic researcher, a Web systems researcher, an AI researcher, a public-service operator, and a resident may all see the same problem differently. A venue focused on data-driven smart cities can make those views comparable by forcing them onto the same chain: what evidence is collected, how it is processed, what decision it supports, and who benefits or is harmed. That is stronger than treating smart cities as a collection of disconnected gadgets. The Web matters because it already connects people, services, data sources, and software interfaces; it can act as the connective layer that lets urban evidence move. The 12th-edition history also matters modestly: a recurring workshop can adjust its focus as the technological pressure changes. In this abstract, the 2026 pressure is the combination of connected devices, AI, agentic AI, integration, and people-centered digital city environments. The approach should improve over the naive dashboard by making methods and their consequences explicit topics of discussion.
po: The payoff is a clearer research agenda for cities that use data as an operating resource rather than a decorative label. Participants can examine how Web technologies help collect, connect, process, and act on urban information, and they can compare how different techniques influence decisions and outcomes. Grounded in the abstract, the promised capability is not a tested system or a numerical gain. It is a forum for understanding how data-driven methods might improve decision-making, optimize city services, and support citizen well-being while acknowledging that the processing choices themselves shape what happens.
limits: The abstract is broad, so it does not prove that any particular smart-city technology improves well-being, saves cost, reduces inequality, or works across cities. It assumes that useful data can be collected and integrated, that the Web can support that integration, and that processing methods can be examined carefully enough to guide better decisions. Those assumptions can fail when data is missing, biased, stale, privately sensitive, or disconnected from residents' lived needs. The workshop framing also leaves open governance questions: who chooses the goals, who audits the methods, and how harms are detected after deployment.
